- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 2–5% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior period), model tends to overcorrect; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 3–5 periods to avoid overshoot.  
- If official supply net is strongly bearish (net < -20) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, model often underestimates downside; add 3–8% downward bias to forecast mean.  
- When sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.33/1.00 alternation), model may misread trend; use 3-period moving average of sentiment to smooth forecast direction.  
- For 30-day forecasts with high event count (≥20 events), reduce forecast slope by 15–25% to account for event-induced volatility and mean reversion.  
- If recent true outcome is significantly lower than forecast (e.g., >10% below), assume model overestimated bullish sentiment; apply downward correction to next forecast mean.  
- When sentiment is low (≤0.33) and true outcome is high, model may be ignoring bearish signals; add 5–10% downward bias to next forecast if sentiment remains low.  
- For 30-day forecasts with high supply net and low bullish sentiment, model often underestimates downside; apply 5–10% downward bias to mean.  
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 3–5 periods.  
- When sentiment is high and true outcome is low, model may be overconfident; reduce forecast slope by 10–15% for next 3–5 periods to account for sentiment misalignment.
